Grant.ProjectTitle: Open Access Edition of Informing a Nation: The Newspaper Presidency of Thomas Jefferson by Mel Laracey
Grant.ProjectDesc: This book illuminates how the third president transformed the relationship between the presidency and the press by using his party newspaper to communicate the administration political agenda to the public while attempting to influence public opinion in favor of his party and against his political opponents.
Grant.ToSupport: No to support statement

Grant.Institution: Sacred Lands Preservation and Education Inc.
Grant.ProjectTitle: Saving Indigenous and Colonial Florida Artifacts from the Storm: Sacred Lands Preservation and Education, Inc. Emergency Response
Grant.Program: Chair's Disaster Recovery Grants for Humanities Collections
Grant.ProjectDesc: Sacred Lands Preservation and Education is based at the Jungle Prada site in St. Petersburg. On the National Register of Historic Places, this site is home to two archeologically-pristine Tocobaga mounds and is recognized as the probable landing of the 1528 Narvaez expedition. Our mission is to preserve and interpret this location and provide educational and cultural programming to the community. But Hurricane Helene drove 8 feet of storm surge onto the property, violently flooding the building that served as museum and event center. Destroyed were flooring, walls, HVAC units, sound and lighting, furniture, and museum display cases. Indigenous and Spanish colonial artifacts were left scattered among the debris. Hurricane Milton delayed recovery by downing more than a dozen trees. Having now recovered the majority of artifacts in our collection, we are seeking funding for their emergency conservation and safe storage, preparation, and display in the aftermath of Helene and Milton.
Grant.ToSupport:
Cleaning and rehousing artifacts damaged and displaced by Hurricanes Helene
and Milton.

Grant.ProjectTitle: A Virtual Ethnographic Investigation at Gold Butte National Monument
Grant.ProjectDesc: The Desert Research Institute (DRI) proposes to create an ethnographic study of the lands within Gold Butte National Monument in collaboration with the Moapa Band of Paiutes. The ethnographic study will be published as an ArcGIS StoryMap where it can be tied to specific locations within the Monument. At the request of the Moapa Band, three virtual tours of locations significant to the Paiute will also be created and embedded into the StoryMap to provide additional context to the ethnography and to provide a form of access for tribal elders who can no longer reach these remote locations. As a digital tool, the ethnographic study will preserve the Moapa Band’s affiliation with the Monument in a way that is accessible for free to anyone with an internet connection.
Grant.ToSupport:
Research and writing leading to a website on indigenous
rock writing in the lands within Gold Butte National Monument, Nevada. (30 months)

Grant.Institution: Curators of the University of Missouri
Grant.ProjectTitle: Recreating Urban Biographies in Roman Italy: The Gabii Project Reports
Grant.ProjectDesc: The proposal is centered on the investigation of Gabii, a Latin town near Rome, Italy, whose exceptionally preserved archaeological sequence spans 1500 years of history from the early Iron Age to Late Antiquity. The aim of the collaborative research is to analyze, interpret, and contextualize the evidence produced through the excavation of a large transect of the site, completed in 2023. The results will be presented in three digital-born scholarly publications that will shine a light on the early beginnings of Gabii, the initial wave of its urbanization, the formation of both civic and commercial infrastructure, and their later repurposing prior to final abandonment. While connecting the findings with contemporary debates about urban life, these scholarly products will also advance practices in the digital publishing of archaeological data in which narrative and 3D visualization are combined in interactive ways.
Grant.ToSupport:
Research and writing leading to three digital
publications on Roman urbanism through the history and archaeology of Gabii,
Italy (c. 800 BCE-700 CE). (36 months)

Participant.Institution: Curators of the University of Missouri

Grant.ProjectTitle: NEH-HFRI: Aristotelian 'Paideia' and Global Educational Challenges: Revisiting the Past to Plan for Sustainable Education in the 21st-Century
Grant.ProjectDesc: As part of the new partnership between the NEH (National Endowment of the Humanities) and HFRI (Hellenic Foundation for Research and Innovation), our project brings together institutions from the U.S. and Greece to explore insights gained from the ancient Greek philosopher Aristotle on education, well-being, ethics, politics, and their interconnections.  Using these insights it aims to create a novel framework for "sustainable education," a concept in educational psychology, to propose an idea for “quality education,” Sustainable Development Goal 4 of the United Nations 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, that cultivates intellect, character, and citizenship in young people today. Our project demonstrates the essential role of the humanities in addressing contemporary society's greatest challenges and strengthens interdisciplinary collaboration between philosophy and educational psychology, promoting a holistic, values-based approach to education and personal development.

Grant.ProjectTitle: Principia Mathematica's Second Edition in Its Century, 1925-2025
Grant.ProjectDesc: This proposal for a Convening Grant would bring together 12-to-15 scholars from philosophy, history, mathematics, and digital humanities for a week to conduct archival research and a collaborative workshop at the Bertrand Russell Archives and Research Centre at McMaster University in Hamilton, Ontario, Canada. The central texts and tools for the workshop will be the NEH-funded edition of Principia Mathematica with its new editorial apparatus and textual notes, the NEH-funded Principia Mathematica Maps and Table Site (PM-MATS), and the holdings of the Bertrand Russell Archives. The outcomes of this Convening grant will be an edited volume with an academic press (likely Cambridge University Press, who have expressed interest), plus increased familiarity and facility of scholars with two NEH-funded work products—the new edition of Principia and the PM-MATS digital resource. The grant period will last January-August 2026.
Grant.ToSupport: Planning and holding a workshop on Principia Mathematica (1910-1913), a foundational text on mathematical logic by British philosophers Alfred North Whitehead (1861-1947) and Bertrand Russell (1872-1970). (8 months)

Grant.ProjectTitle: Mapping Links between Architectural Comparanda in Greco-Roman Architecture for Knowledge Discovery with Machine Learning
Grant.ProjectDesc: This application fits in the funding category of scholarly digital projects. This project aims to create a network of ancient Greek and Roman buildings, represented by nodes and linked to their “architectural comparanda,” to assist in the reconstruction and interpretation process of each of these buildings. We propose to use generative AI to analyze, at scale, publicly available archaeological records created manually by disjoint teams of archaeologists over decades. These records contain, firstly, documentation of the state of preservation of fragmentary remains of ancient buildings in several sites, in the form of images, drawings, measurements, and free form text, and, secondly, proposed reconstructions of architectural plans based on this data as well as evidence from “architectural comparanda,” i.e. other comparable parallel or precedent buildings, belonging to the same geographic region, period, patronage, type or style.

Grant.ProjectTitle: Pandemic and History: Disease, Myth, and the End of Antiquity
Grant.ProjectDesc: This project investigates how a pandemic became conceptualized as a key motor of historical change leading to the ancient world’s end. The first part explores the social, cultural, and environmental effects of the first plague pandemic (541-750 CE). By examining multidisciplinary data, it reevaluates the popular narrative of widespread collapse and proposes a framework of societal resilience. It then explores how people developed new cultural understandings to cope with later plague outbreaks. The second part traces the creation and growth of the catastrophic narrative over the last 150 years that turned it into a model for future pandemic responses. It uncovers how colonial officials constructed a myth about the ancient plague’s impact to demonstrate their scientific power to conquer late 19th century outbreaks. The project demonstrates how the biomedical conquest myth persists up to the Covid pandemic, decentering human impacts in favor of debates about hypothetical societal collapse.
Grant.ToSupport:
Research and writing leading to a co-authored book on the
first plague pandemic (c. 541-750 CE) and the evolution of narratives about it. (36 months)

Grant.ProjectTitle: NEH-HFRI: The Archaeology of Small Islands in the Northeast Mediterranean
Grant.ProjectDesc: Islands occupy a special place in the history of human societies and in contemporary cultural imaginations. In the ancient world, island life included sanctuaries, settlements, trade systems, and legendary points of reference. Island archaeology, now a well-established subfield of archaeology, has brought significant advances to our understanding of human migration, evolution, and social complexity. Yet small islands are regularly left out of the picture, due to the particular challenges of human occupation and carrying out research on them. Nevertheless, small islands shed light on some of the least known patterns and scales of human adaptability, endurance, and activity in marginal environments from prehistoric to modern times. This collaborative project brings together researchers from the U.S., Greece, and elsewhere to develop new methodological and comparative frameworks for small-island studies based on recent research in Greece, one of the world’s most significant island theaters.
Grant.ToSupport:
Planning and holding an international conference on the
archaeology of small islands in the Mediterranean. (12 months)

Grant.ProjectTitle: Focusing Policy for Good: Promoting Al for Good for the Disability Community
Grant.ProjectDesc: We propose a convening that will bring together scholars and community members to discuss artificial intelligence (AI) for good in healthcare and education to serve the disability community. While AI is a controversial topic, there are a few uses of AI that tend to be considered obviously good use cases. One of those use cases is creating tools for people with disabilities (e.g., apps that read written text aloud for those with low vision). While these tools are frequently mentioned by those who are creating AI tools, most of the effort in the AI field is to create those things that either have some immediate payoff for the startups that create them (e.g., business or educational technology tools) or that intrigue venture capitalists such that they need not be profitable for the foreseeable future (e.g., ChatGPT). Our idea is to critically examine the tools that have been created, the possibilities for the future, and the policies and economic incentives that might encourage AI for good.
Grant.ToSupport: Planning and holding a conference on positive AI interventions for the disability community. (12 months)

Grant.ProjectTitle: Volume 13 of “The Complete Works of Jack London”
Grant.ProjectDesc: Volume 13 contains two works by Jack London: The Cruise of the Snark and South Sea Tales. The former is a nonfictional account of his voyage on the Snark from San Francisco to Sydney in 1907 to 1909. The latter is a fictional account of those same travels. This truly collaborative project will be conducted by Jay Williams, the general editor of The Complete Works of Jack London and the volume’s textual editor; Professor Amy Tucker, the volume editor; and Ward Eldridge, archivist at Cal State Parks, who will provide new, high-resolution of the volume’s 120 photos taken by London.
Grant.ToSupport: Preparation for publication of volume 13 of The Complete Works of Jack London, containing critical editions of The Cruise of the Snark (1911) and South Sea Tales (1911). (24 months)

Grant.ProjectTitle: A Critical Edition of the Works of George Gershwin (1898-1937) and Ira Gershwin (1896-1983)
Grant.ProjectDesc: Launched in 2015, the George and Ira Gershwin Critical Edition is an international, collaborative project that aims to produce the first-ever accurate and academically rigorous critical scores of the complete works of George and Ira Gershwin, including some fifty volumes of the brothers’ songs, film scores, operas, Broadway and Hollywood musicals, writings, and correspondence, as well as George Gershwin’s instrumental works for orchestra, string quartet, and keyboard. The all-new edition facilitates both study and performance, giving a wide audience—conductors, musicians, performers, scholars, students, enthusiasts, and the public alike—greater insight into the Gershwins’ creative output.
Grant.ToSupport: Preparation for publication of a critical edition of the performance scores of the works of George Gershwin (1898-1937) and Ira Gershwin (1896-1983), including Porgy and Bess and The Gershwin Song-Book. (36 months)

Grant.ProjectTitle: Jane Addams Papers Project
Grant.ProjectDesc: The digital edition of the Jane Addams Papers Project broadens scholarly access, allowing far deeper searches than are possible using the microfilm or scattered archival holdings.  The JAPP’s goals for 2025-2028 are to digitize, describe, and transcribe documents from 1931 to 1934 in JADE (approximately 3,600 documents), submit the completed Volume 6 manuscript to the press, and begin annotation research on Volume 7.
Grant.ToSupport:
Preparation
for publication of volumes 6 and 7 of the selected papers and a digital
edition of letters of social reformer Jane Addams (1860-1935). (36 months)

Grant.ProjectTitle: The Glossa Ordinaria: Translation and Annotation of the Standard Medieval Bible Commentary
Grant.ProjectDesc: The Glossa Ordinaria (“Standard Gloss”) was the most popular and influential medieval commentary on the Bible. Compiled in the twelfth century, it consists of a running, verse-by-verse commentary on the entire Bible. The glosses (“interpretive notes”) are famously displayed in an ingenious format, with the biblical text spaciously written in the center column, flanked by longer marginal glosses on either side, and interwoven with shorter glosses between the lines. Although first devised as a classroom textbook for lecture courses on the Bible, it soon became a standard work of reference, and it exerted a significant influence over the subsequent development of medieval university education. This project will support the translation and annotation of eight volumes of the Glossa Ordinaria as part of a larger twenty-volume series, which will provide readers with the first English translation of the complete text.
Grant.ToSupport:
Preparation for publication of a
translation of eight volumes of a 12th-century commentary on the Bible. (36
months)

Grant.ProjectTitle: A New Critical Edition of John Lydgate's Shorter Works: Popular Culture and Lyric Poetry in the Later Middle Ages
Grant.ProjectDesc: This grant will support the production of a new critical edition of the shorter works of John Lydgate, to be published by the Early English Text Society in cooperation with Oxford University Press. Lydgate was the most important Middle English poet of the fifteenth century and, thanks to his work as a poet, dramatist, and translator, he serves as the central node in the socio-literary networks crisscrossing fifteenth-century England. In the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, Lydgate’s reputation and fame hinged upon the brief lyrics and poems of instruction that can be found everywhere in the collections of medieval and early modern readers. So popular were these shorter poems that their dissemination introduced a universe of learning to an English reading public that was clearly hungry for it. For this same reason, the shorter works remain important today—and not just to scholars of Middle English, but to scholars of medieval religion, history, and other European literatures.
Grant.ToSupport:
Preparation for publication of a two-volume,
critical edition of the shorter works of English poet and monk John Lydgate (1370-1451).
(36 months)

Grant.ProjectTitle: The Collected Letters of May Morris
Grant.ProjectDesc: This proposal seeks NEH funding in support of the planning phase of an international project to locate, transcribe, annotate, and publish the letters of artist and editor May Morris (1862–1938), a leading artist in the British Arts & Crafts movement, a pioneer of ‘art embroidery’ and an influential teacher and author who lectured in both the UK and US. Widely dispersed, the letters are located in archives and private collections across the UK, US, and Europe, including sizeable holdings at the British Library and William Morris Gallery in London, the International Institute for Social History in Amsterdam, and the Huntington Library in San Marino, CA. The Delaware Art Museum, institutional host for this application, houses the largest collection of Pre-Raphaelite and Arts & Crafts objects in the United States. As such, fostering scholarship in Victorian studies is critical within the Museum’s curatorial mandate.
Grant.ToSupport:
Preparation for publication of an edition
of the selected letters of British artist and editor May Morris (1862-1938). (12
months)

Grant.ProjectTitle: Digital Dickens Notes Project
Grant.ProjectDesc: The Digital Dickens Notes Project is an open-access digital scholarly edition of the detailed working notes Charles Dickens kept for his novels in the second half of his career. These texts constitute a unique archive essential to understanding this major author’s navigation of serial writing in installments over many months. In addition to offering valuable insights into individual novels, these documents shed light on the development of serial narrative form in the 19th century. Our interactive edition presents visually-faithful transcriptions of Dickens’s manuscripts and comprehensive annotations to capture Dickens’s dynamic use of these pages before, during, and after writing his installments. This grant supports the completion of the project: the publication of the remaining four editions of Notes (Dombey & Son, Our Mutual Friend, The Mystery of Edwin Drood, and an edition of fragmentary planning documents for three other novels), and the integration of manuscript photographs.
Grant.ToSupport:
Preparation for publication of an open-access
edition of the working notes for three novels by British writer Charles Dickens
(1812-1870). (24 months)

Grant.ProjectTitle: The History of the Patriarchs of the East: Eastern Christianity from Ancient Persia to Medieval Islam. An Annotated Translation of the Ecclesiastical History in The Book of the Tower.
Grant.ProjectDesc: This project will produce an annotated English translation of the only complete, surviving account of the Church of the East across its first millennium: the ecclesiastical history found in the medieval theological compendium called The Book of the Tower. This translation will make accessible to students, researchers, and general readers an important but little-known chapter in the histories of Christianity, the medieval Middle East, the city of Baghdad, and Christian-Muslim relations. It includes the complex relationship between the early Muslim caliphs and the largest Christian community under their authority. In addition, ours will be among the first complete, annotated English translations of a major Christian Arabic historical work. As such, it will draw attention to a substantial but neglected strand of Middle Eastern historical writing.
Grant.ToSupport:
Preparation for publication of a translation of a history of the Eastern
Christian Church written in Arabic around the 10th century. (36 months)

Grant.ProjectTitle: The Amy Lowell Letters Project
Grant.ProjectDesc: We seek an NEH Scholarly Editions Implementation grant for work on The Amy Lowell Letters Project, an open-access, digital scholarly edition of the never before collected letters of American poet, editor, and critic Amy Lowell (1874–1925).
Grant.ToSupport:
Preparation for publication of an open-access,
digital edition of the letters of American poet, editor, and critic Amy Lowell
(1874–1925). (36 months)

Grant.ProjectTitle: The Correspondence of Zachary Taylor and Millard Fillmore
Grant.ProjectDesc: The Correspondence of Zachary Taylor and Millard Fillmore, a project of American University’s Center for Congressional and Presidential Studies, is creating a digital and print edition of letters by and to the twelfth and thirteenth US presidents. Its editors and student assistants are locating, transcribing, annotating, and publishing letters of the decade when Taylor and Fillmore played their largest national roles: from 1844, when Taylor prepared to lead troops into Texas, through 1849 and 1850, when Taylor and then Fillmore became president, to 1853, when Fillmore retired from the White House. These two men wrote hundreds of letters on Texas annexation, the Mexican-American War, social challenges facing the United States, and their personal hopes and struggles. Others wrote them thousands of letters—men and women and children, Blacks and Whites and Native Americans, businessmen and laborers and farmers, Whigs and Democrats and abolitionists.
Grant.ToSupport:
Preparation for publication of an edition of the letters sent and received by the 12th president, Zachary Taylor (1784–1850), and 13th president, Millard Fillmore (1800–1874).
(24 months)

Grant.ProjectTitle: Freedmen and Southern Society Project
Grant.ProjectDesc: The Freedmen and Southern Society Project is editing Freedom: A Documentary History of Emancipation, 1861-1867, a ten-volume documentary history of the transition from slavery to freedom in the U.S. South. The edition documents a critical juncture in American history: the moment four million slaves gained their freedom. It constitutes a social history in the words of emancipated slaves and their contemporaries. Eight volumes will have been completed by the beginning of the proposed grant period. The ninth and tenth volumes will be the work of the proposed grant period. The editors have published four additional volumes for general audiences and use in the classroom. The project's website provides both documents and interpretive material.
Grant.ToSupport: Preparation for publication of volumes 9 and 10 of Freedom: A Documentary History of Emancipation, 1861-1867. (36 months)

Grant.ProjectTitle: "Missing Me One Place, Search Another": Locating and Digitally Editing Walt Whitman's Unsigned Journalism (1846-48)
Grant.ProjectDesc: Making use of innovative authorship attribution methods, we propose to create an annotated digital edition of Whitman's journalistic writings from 1846–1848, one of his most prolific periods, when he was principally employed as editor of the Brooklyn Daily Eagle. Based on recent discoveries by our team, we also suspect that Whitman was contributing to other papers (particularly weekend papers) at the same time. We therefore anticipate including a significant batch of material from this time period that has heretofore not been attributed to Whitman. When completed, the edition—which we anticipate will encompass roughly 1,000 editorials—will be published and freely available on the online Walt Whitman Archive (WWA), where it will join a growing trove of Whitman's journalistic writings that exist beside and in conversation with other Whitman-authored texts on the WWA site.
Grant.ToSupport: Preparation for publication of the journalistic writing of Walt Whitman (1819-1892) while editor of the Brooklyn Daily Eagle. (36 months)

Grant.ProjectTitle: Frederick Douglass Papers Digital Edition
Grant.ProjectDesc: The Frederick Douglass Papers Digital Edition’s mission is to make verified transcriptions of all of the more than 13,000 texts of the speeches, autobiographies, correspondence, and journalism and other writings of the iconic nineteenth century African American Frederick Douglass accessible to scholars, teachers, students, and general readers in an electronically searchable and easily downloadable format on the project’s free public access website. The current application seeks support to prepare verified transcriptions along with annotation and other scholarly apparatus for  c.2,500 of Douglass’s speeches (1841-1895).
Grant.ToSupport:
Preparation for publication of an
online resource of more than 13,000 speeches, letters, and other writings of
the African American social reformer and statesman, Frederick Douglass
(1818-1895). (36 months)

Grant.ProjectTitle: Library of Babylonian Literature
Grant.ProjectDesc: Babylonian literature is a treasure trove of poetic gems, but only a few are known outside the discipline of Assyriology. While students of world literature may have heard of Gilgamesh, they are often surprised to discover that Babylonian poetry is much richer and more diverse than the fame of this single text would suggest. Babylonian literature had a crucial effect on the making of the Hebrew Bible and may have influenced Classical literature as well, making it the hidden foundation of Western culture. The Library of Babylonian Literature (LBL) aims to make the major works of literature in the Akkadian language more accessible to students, scholars, and first-time readers. Each volume presents one or more Babylonian poems in an updated transcription, an accessible and elegant translation, an introduction that presents the significance and historical background of the work, and a series of essays by leading scholars that guide new readers through its most important facets.
Grant.ToSupport:
Preparation for publication of critical editions of ancient Babylonian literature with English
translations. (36 months)

Grant.ProjectTitle: The Papers of Thomas Jefferson
Grant.ProjectDesc:
The
Papers of Thomas Jefferson editorial project at Princeton University seeks an implementation
award for continuing work on the authoritative scholarly edition of papers by
and to Thomas Jefferson (1743–1826). By the start of the requested grant on 1
January 2026, the edition will have published 49 chronological volumes that
span from January 1760 to early July 1806. During the performance period the
editorial staff will be preparing and publishing documents from Jefferson’s
second term as president of the United States.
Grant.ToSupport:
Preparation
for publication of print volumes 50 through 58 and digital publication of
volumes 48 through 50 of the papers of Thomas Jefferson (1743–1826). (36
months)

Grant.ProjectTitle: Letters of American Author Catharine Maria Sedgwick (1789-1867): An Online Edition
Grant.ProjectDesc: The Catharine Maria Sedgwick Online Letters Project (CMSOL) seeks to publish an open-access digital edition of the complete, unexpurgated letters written by Sedgwick (1789-1867) to her more than 250 correspondents over seven decades. This phase of the project begins in 1837 and continues through 1846. Sedgwick's literary status as the premier American woman writer of the Early National Period as well as her contributions to the most important cultural and political conversations of the day argue for the publication of this heretofore unpublished personal correspondence.
Grant.ToSupport:
Preparation for publication of an open-access,
digital edition of the complete letters of early American writer Catharine
Maria Sedgwick (1789-1867). (36 months)

Grant.ProjectTitle: Nietzsche, Unpublished Fragments from the Period of The Birth of Tragedy
Grant.ProjectDesc: These notes stem from the time of his first book, The Birth of Tragedy, and include material that expands upon and reimagines that influential work. Continuations of other unpublished works like On the Future of Our Educational Institutions and Philosophy in the Tragic Age of the Greeks are also proposed. In these notebooks, we see Nietzsche come to characterize his thinking as an inversion of Plato. Across these pages we also encounter material not found in his other works, like sketches for a play on the ancient Greek philosopher Empedocles, a deeper engagement with ancient Greek sources in the original language, as well as poetic compositions, and musical sketches of Nietzsche’s own. Lastly, the notebooks are records of Nietzsche’s biography, from his teaching schedules and lists of amounts owed or pages written to the notebook he kept while driving an ambulance in the Franco-Prussian war.
Grant.ToSupport: Preparation for publication of an English translation of the Unpublished Fragments from the Period of “The Birth of Tragedy,” volume 10 of The Complete Works of Friedrich Nietzsche (1844–1900). (12 months)

Grant.ProjectTitle: Naval Documents of the American Revolution
Grant.ProjectDesc: The Naval Documents of the American Revolution project at the Center for Digital Editing is a scholarly digital editing project with the mission of creating an edition that provides a comprehensive overview of the American Revolution at sea. The collection includes American, British, Dutch, French, and Spanish points of view and gives voice to common seamen, civilians, women, and enslaved people, as well as policymakers, political leaders, and naval and military officers. NDAR’s corpus of documents represents the most extensive collection of source materials on the naval war of the American Revolution in existence.
Grant.ToSupport:
Preparation for publication of an open-access
edition of documents related to the naval history of the American Revolution.
(36 months)

Participant.Institution: Rector and Visitors of the University of Virginia

Grant.ProjectTitle: Aristotle’s Poetics in Greek, Arabic and Latin: Towards a Variorum Edition
Grant.ProjectDesc: The project aims to create a digital edition of Aristotle’s Poetics in Greek, Arabic, and Latin, blending traditional philology with digital humanities to enhance access and bridge linguistic barriers. Richly annotated translations aligned with original texts will allow researchers without expertise in these languages to explore term usage, syntax, and cultural reception. It addresses critical gaps in Poetics scholarship, focusing on the 10th-century Arabic translation by Abu-Bishr Matta, the 13th-century Latin by William of Moerbeke, and the Translation Movements of Baghdad (9th-10th CE) and Toledo (12th-13th CE). The openly accessible, born-digital edition will feature translation alignments, linguistic annotations, and commentaries, hosted on the Perseus Digital Library, enabling global engagement with Aristotle’s influential work.
Grant.ToSupport: Preparation for publication of an online digital edition and translation of Aristotle’s Poetics (circa 335 BC), the earliest work of Greek dramatic theory. (36 months)

Grant.ProjectTitle: Adams Papers Editorial Project
Grant.ProjectDesc: The Adams Papers Editorial Project at the Massachusetts Historical Society (MHS) is the authoritative scholarly edition of the diaries, letters, official records, public writings, and literary miscellanies written by three generations of the Adams family of Massachusetts, including Abigail Adams, John Adams, John Quincy Adams, Charles Francis Adams, and their families. Based on the Adams Family Papers collection at the MHS and supplemented by Adams manuscripts in other archives, this family record charts the changes that transformed American life between the American Revolution and the Civil War. Since 1961, the project has published 59 volumes, with 52 freely available online. Editors are focused on the founding generation’s efforts to establish the American union, a complex saga that will unfold by 2040. The Adams Papers has received the aid of the NEH continuously since 2003, and we seek further support to make this unparalleled resource accessible to all.
Grant.ToSupport:
Preparation for publication of volumes
23 and 24 of the papers of John Adams (1735-1826) and volumes 17 and 18 of the
Adams family’s correspondence. (24 months)

Grant.ProjectTitle: “Center for Humanistic Inquiry into AI and Uncertainty" at University of Wisconsin - Madison
Grant.Program: Humanities Research Centers on Artificial Intelligence
Grant.ProjectDesc: The “Center for Humanistic Inquiry into AI and Uncertainty” is a research center dedicated to investigating the multifaceted dimensions of uncertainty in emerging AI technologies and anticipating future harms and risks posed by these technologies. The Center advances its iterative and anticipatory research mission by providing a community of multidisciplinary humanities scholars with resources for producing impactful research for scholars and the wider public. With the support of the Project Director, an Advisory Board of humanities leaders, and a Steering Committee, Center Fellows engage in individual and collaborative research around annually rotating research questions keyed to the themes of power, knowledge, and creativity, and issue an annual whitepaper identifying pressing issues in AI and its impact on society. In every other year, Fellows convene a Public Forum for industry practitioners, representatives from local and national organizations, and community members.
Grant.ToSupport: Establishing a humanities research center at the University of Wisconsin on AI and uncertainty, with particular attention to themes of power, knowledge, and creativity. (36 months)

Grant.ProjectTitle: Georgetown University’s Initiative on Artificial Intelligence and Democratic Citizenship
Grant.Program: Humanities Research Centers on Artificial Intelligence
Grant.ProjectDesc: Georgetown University’s Initiative on Artificial Intelligence and Democratic Citizenship (AIDC) is designed to produce impactful research addressing the effects that AI has on the individual’s experience of democratic life. In partnership with Georgetown’s Humanities Initiative and the Aspen Institute, AIDC will create an interdisciplinary network of DC-area scholars who seek to turn their humanistic expertise into practical, accessible insights. Collectively, they will work to illuminate the transformative impact AI poses for the future of democratic self-governance, including both the obstacles it presents for maintaining democratic traditions as well as the opportunities it offers for the extension and innovation of democratic practices. Toward these ends, AIDC will sponsor annual fellowships and monthly public events to produce cutting-edge academic research aimed at advancing humanistic scholarship on AI and to facilitate the dissemination of these insights to a broader audience.
Grant.ToSupport: Establishing a humanities research center at Georgetown University exploring the effects of AI on the individual’s experience of democratic life. (36 months)

Grant.ProjectTitle: University of Cincinnati Center for Explainable, Ethical, and Trustworthy AI
Grant.Program: Humanities Research Centers on Artificial Intelligence
Grant.ProjectDesc: CEET’s overall mission is to explore issues of explainability, ethics, and trust in AI. This mission will be served by two complementary units: a research unit which will develop humanities-based perspectives on these themes, and a public engagement unit which will develop educational materials and disseminate results to both educational and public audiences.
Grant.ToSupport: Establishing a humanities research center at the University of Cincinnati on explainability, ethics, and trust in AI. (36 months)

Grant.ProjectTitle: Notre Dame Program on AI and the Development of Ethics In Agents (ND-PAIDEIA)
Grant.Program: Humanities Research Centers on Artificial Intelligence
Grant.ProjectDesc: The Notre Dame Program on AI and the Development of Ethics in Agents (ND-PAIDEIA) will gather a multidisciplinary team of scholars to explore how virtue ethics can inform the development, implementation, assessment, and use of generative AI systems. ND-PAIDEIA will create a virtue-based framework for approaching generative AI that will then be refined through two applied projects: AI systems in local government and the use of generative AI for translation. Those applications arise from the two central themes for the center: (1) Generative AI, Citizenship & Justice and (2) Generative AI, Creativity, & Human Judgment. Together, these themes reflect fundamental questions about the place of the humanities amidst the growing technological power of AI: how can the humanities inform our use and design of generative AI systems, and how can reflection on the capabilities of generative AI clarify or develop our understanding of what, if anything, is distinctively human about the humanities?
Grant.ToSupport: Establishing a humanities research center at the University of Notre Dame to explore how the humanities, particularly the notion of virtue ethics, can inform the use and design of generative AI systems. (36 months)

Grant.ProjectTitle: Center for Humanities-based Health AI Innovation (CHHAIN)
Grant.Program: Humanities Research Centers on Artificial Intelligence
Grant.ProjectDesc: We propose to create the first Center for Humanities-based Health AI Innovation (CHHAIN) to fill pressing knowledge gaps by rigorously advancing humanities research, translation and public education/outreach with a thematic focus on trustworthy health AI innovation theory and practice.
Grant.ToSupport: Establishing a collaborative humanities research center at Baylor College of Medicine and Rice University focused on integrating humanities knowledge into the development of trustworthy AI tools in the health sector. (36 months)

Grant.ProjectTitle: Emancipation Summer: The Meaning of Freedom in Mississippi
Grant.Program: Cooperative Agreements and Special Projects (Public Programs)
Grant.ProjectDesc: This project will explore the history and legacy of the end of enslavement in Mississippi with public programs in three different towns that were sites of major events in the story of freedom’s expansion and contraction. Through commemorations, lectures, living history demonstrations, and historic tours organized by three different Black-led museums, this project will foster a greater public understanding of a transformative moment in American history. While Juneteenth commemorates the news of slavery’s end in Texas, Black communities in Mississippi have been marking their own communities’ histories of emancipation and freedom for over a century, and our project aims to support and build upon these local efforts.

Grant.ProjectTitle: Expanded and Enhanced Juneteenth Commemoration at historic Catoctin Furnace
Grant.Program: Cooperative Agreements and Special Projects (Public Programs)
Grant.ProjectDesc: The Catoctin Furnace Historical Society, Inc. (CFHS) is seeking $30,000 of funding to design, plan, implement, and evaluate expanded Juneteenth programming at Catoctin Furnace for 2025 as a part of our ongoing descendant communication and inclusion initiative. As you are aware, with NEH funding, a descendant communicator position has been in place during calendar year 2024 to help manage the overwhelming response to the August 4, 2023 Science article and resultant media exposure.  As that position draws to a close, this expanded Juneteenth commemoration will continue the momentum, communication, research, and coordination with the descendant community and culminating in a 5th annual Juneteenth commemoration at Catoctin.

Grant.ProjectTitle: Juneteenth in Germantown

Smith, a community zine-making workshop facilitated by Smith, and a history-based panel discussion on the legacy of the Johnson’s House Historic Site's abolitionist roots as connected to social movements over the past 175 years.

Grant.ProjectTitle: National Center for Civil and Human Rights’ Juneteenth Commemoration in Atlanta
Grant.Program: Cooperative Agreements and Special Projects (Public Programs)
Grant.ProjectDesc: The National Center for Civil and Human Rights (the Center) proposes a commemorative and educational family-centered celebration of Juneteenth using multiple activations to expose and deepen the general public’s knowledge and celebration of Juneteenth as a major event in American history. Attendees will increase their understanding of the importance of Juneteenth and its impact on celebrations of freedom.

Grant.ProjectDesc: The Fredericksburg Area Museum (FAM) seeks funding in the amount of $23,500 for the development of Juneteenth: Honoring Our Wazee (Elders), a program series commemorating the 160th anniversary of Juneteenth. This community series will feature programs engaging a wide variety of ages and backgrounds, including a community lecture on the history of Juneteenth, a family program detailing emancipation stories, and an all-day community Juneteenth celebration.

Grant.ProjectTitle: J.O.Y. | Juneteenth on the Yard
Grant.Program: Cooperative Agreements and Special Projects (Public Programs)
Grant.ProjectDesc: “J.O.Y. | Juneteenth on the Yard," provides a joyful afternoon of music, dance, and festivities held in the African Ancestors Memorial Garden at the International African American Museum, fusing critically important history with contemporary expression. By honoring this historic day, we not only commemorate the legacy of those who came before us but also inspire future generations to continue the pursuit of freedom.
Grant.ToSupport: No to support statement

Grant.ProjectTitle: The Black Struggle for Freedom Before and After Juneteenth
Grant.Program: Cooperative Agreements and Special Projects (Public Programs)
Grant.ProjectDesc: The Penn Center National Historic Landmark District (https://www.penncenter.com/) will celebrate Juneteenth on June 19, 2025, by hosting several events, free and open to the public, that critically consider the long journey of Black people from slavery to freedom. Juneteenth celebrates the end of African American enslavement, when Major General Gordon Granger of the Union Army issued his General Order No. 3 in Galveston, Texas, on June 19, 1865, manumitting Black people still enslaved in that state. This annual commemoration also has promoted African Americans’ ongoing struggle for equality and the full rights of American citizenship.  Our program will commemorate how Gullah Geechee communities, unique African American cultures in the coastal South and Low Country that date to early sixteenth-century colonization efforts, and communities of the Gullah Geechee diaspora. which extend north into Canada and west into Oklahoma, Texas, and Mexico, have advanced ideas of democracy and freedom

Among the countless women who have challenged traditional gender roles to pursue nontraditional vocations, the women who reported on Vietnam occupy a unique place. Defying societal norms with their unconventional career choice, they confronted boundaries both official and unspoken, as views on women’s roles shifted with the times; taking the full measure of their wartime experience reveals a group of ambitious women who served as a kind of fever chart for changing gender norms in 1960s America. The Women Who Reported Vietnam will explore the work and legacy of these brave and brazen journalists, and how that conflict forever changed the opportunities and image of female war correspondents.

Grant.ProjectDesc: Etruscan culture flourished between the Arno and Tiber rivers in the area we know as Tuscany from the ninth to second centuries BC. The Etruscans were a sophisticated and wealthy people who were major contributors to Western Civilization's most outstanding architectural, engineering, and artistic achievements, yet these great innovators only recently began to be discovered in the United States.   A new exhibition, "The Etruscans: From the Heart of Ancient Italy", will introduce this sophisticated society based on the latest archaeological discoveries and the most up-to-date scholarship. On view at the Legion of Honor from May 2 through September 20, 2026, the exhibition will feature approximately 200 objects renowned for their beauty and craftsmanship. The objects reveal how the achievements of the Etruscans significantly influenced Western civilization, leaving a lasting legacy that still captivates us today.

The project will bring the 1921 Battle of Blair Mountain—the largest armed labor uprising in U.S. history—to life with free interpretive materials and permanent public installations. Grant.ProjectTitle: Shakespeare and Digital Storytelling
Grant.ProjectDesc: Agnes Scott College (ASC) proposes “Shakespeare and Digital Storytelling,” a two-week residential summer institute for a diverse group of 25 English teachers of grades nine through 12. ASC will host the institute June 14–26, 2026, on its campus outside Atlanta, Georgia. Participants will engage in an in-depth study of Shakespeare’s A Midsummer Night’s Dream, The Taming of the Shrew, and Hamlet, exploring the plays’ folk and fairy tale roots and 21st-century approaches to teaching Shakespeare, including digital storytelling. Toby Emert, professor of English education and theater, will serve as project director. The interdisciplinary faculty team will also include a Shakespearean scholar, a professor of art, and an associate professor of history, with additional support from a digital curator, an experienced theater educator, and four accomplished K-12 teachers. Robust post-institute dissemination activities will extend the institute’s impact beyond the in-person participants.
Grant.ToSupport: A two-week residential institute for 25 high school English teachers to study digital storytelling approaches to teaching Shakespeare.

Grant.ProjectTitle: The Ancient Olympics and Daily Life in Ancient Olympia: A Hands-On History
Grant.ProjectDesc: The Ancient Olympics and Daily Life in Ancient Olympia: A Hands-on History will immerse teachers in many aspects of the ancient Olympic Games and the local life going on around those Games through scholarly historical research via original literary sources, visuals of material remains revealed through archaeology, and secondary analysis from contemporary scholars. More importantly, though, this institute will help participants to understand the Games and ancient Mediterranean life in hands-on fashion, teaching participants how to do the Olympic events in the ancient style, to carry out the work of artisans and craftspeople of the time, and more broadly to experience the materiality of ancient life. The proposed institute will be residential so that participants can engage in the physical component of the institute that is so important to its impact, and so that they can take advantage of Monmouth College’s excellent facilities for this purpose.
Grant.ToSupport: A two-week residential institute for 26 K-12 teachers on the ancient Olympics and ancient Mediterranean life.

Grant.Institution: Theatre for a New Audience, Inc.
Grant.ProjectTitle: TFANA's Summer Institute: Scholarship and Performance, A Combined Approach to Teaching Shakespeare’s Plays
Grant.ProjectDesc: Theatre for a New Audience (TFANA) proposes a two-week Summer Institute entitled Scholarship and Performance: A Combined Approach to Teaching Shakespeare’s Plays, to be held July 13-24, 2026 at Polonsky Shakespeare Center in Brooklyn, New York. Offered to a national group of 25 middle and high school teachers, the Institute uses a integrated approach for exploring text-based scholarship, contextual and original source material, language, and performance in two of Shakespeare plays, as well as cross-disciplinary and contemporary issues illuminated by the plays’ content. For this year’s theme, “Witches, Warriors, and Counselors: Shakespeare’s Women in Times of War,” participants will study MACBETH and HENRY VI (PART 1) with leading Shakespeare scholars Julie Crawford (Columbia University), Mario DiGangi (Lehman College and the Graduate Center, City University of New York), master teaching artists and theatre practitioners Krista Apple and Claudia Zelevansky, and K-12 leader Maria Fahey.
Grant.ToSupport: A two-week institute for 25 middle and high school teachers on two plays by Shakespeare.

Participant.Institution: Theatre for a New Audience, Inc.
Trustees of Columbia University in the City of New York

Grant.ProjectTitle: Emily Dickinson Museum, ‘Revolution is the Pod’: Emily Dickinson’s American Poetry
Grant.Program: Landmarks of American History and Culture for K-12 Educators
Grant.ProjectDesc: The Emily Dickinson Museum proposes a Landmarks of American History and Culture Workshop for K-12 educators, ‘Revolution is the Pod’: Emily Dickinson’s American Poetry, in summer 2026. This workshop will examine Dickinson’s poetry in light of the rhetoric of her day, as Americans grappled with a national identity one century on from the American Revolution. Through creative writing and engagement with contemporary poets, participants will also explore how Dickinson’s rule-breaking, revolutionary poetry sparks the imaginations of new generations. The workshop will consist of two one-week sessions for thirty-six teachers each, Session I: July 19-24, 2026 and Session II: July 26-31, 2026. Participants will be based at Amherst College, parent organization of the Emily Dickinson Museum. The Museum received this grant previously in 2009, 2011, 2014, and 2017, holding a workshop called “Emily Dickinson: Person, Poetry, and Place”.
Grant.ToSupport: Two week-long residential workshops for cohorts of 36 K-12 educators each on Emily Dickinson’s poetry.

Grant.ProjectTitle: Schenectady Celebrates 250!
Grant.Program: Cooperative Agreements and Special Projects (Challenge Grants)
Grant.ProjectDesc: Schenectady Celebrates 250! is a year-long project featuring an exhibition, a symposium, and public programs (reading/ discussion series, theater performance, large community events and small family programs) that will both celebrate the commemoration of America’s 250th birthday, and explore and interpret important topics in American revolutionary history, including the founding of America, our nation’s milestones and progress, and the power of place in Schenectady.
Grant.ToSupport:
An exhibition showcasing Schenectady’s 1771
Liberty Flag, as well as a related symposium and public programs on topics in
American revolutionary history in Schenectady, New York.

Grant.ProjectTitle: John Adams and the Cradle of Liberty
Grant.ProjectDesc: The key themes and topics we would hope to explore through the project's events include the life and times of the Founding’s pivotal intellectual and political figure, John Adams, and his wife, and our namesake, Abigail Adams. Our primary interest is in the question of American exceptionalism, with a focus on the revolutionary Founding. The works of John Adams in constitutional theory serve as the high point of this project. Leading up to it, we are eager to explore what he read and how he integrated the ideas of luminaries such as Montesquieu. Equally important, we would like to focus on his personal formation, his close relationship with Abigail, and how they built an American dynasty. The final parts of our explorations would focus on John Adams’ specifically American legacy, and larger impact on our public life.
Grant.ToSupport:
A series of events, to include public lectures, seminars, a
film viewing, and tours of historic sites and archives, focused on the work and
legacy of John Adams.

Grant.ProjectTitle: Lost Region Recovery Project (LRRP)
Grant.ProjectDesc: Scholars and writers in the American Midwest have in recent years attempted to jumpstart the study of the interior of the country. Specifically, they have attempted to revive Midwestern history, a field which fell dormant for decades. To assess their progress and map out an agenda for future work, these scholars will assemble together in Sioux Falls in October of 2025 and hold a conference. The results of this conference will be published in the academic journal Middle West Review.
Grant.ToSupport: No to support statement

Grant.ProjectTitle: Meritocracy vs. Equity: The Declaration of Independence in Tension with Critical Race Theory and DEI
Grant.ProjectDesc: I propose a research project under the auspices of the National Endowment for the Humanities to investigate a profound philosophical and practical conflict shaping our nation’s civic discourse: the Declaration of Independence’s call for meritocracy versus the equity-driven imperatives of Critical Race Theory (CRT) and Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI) policies. This study seeks to illuminate the intellectual roots, historical implications, and contemporary stakes of this tension, offering a rigorous analysis grounded in primary texts and public policy outcomes.
Grant.ToSupport: Research and writing of a book on the political theories behind the Declaration of Independence and Critical Race Theory.

Grant.ProjectTitle: Digital Humanities of the American Revolution fortification at Butts Hill (Portsmouth, Rhode Island)
Grant.Program: Cooperative Agreements and Special Projects (Challenge Grants)
Grant.ProjectDesc: This project will conduct non-destructive archaeological imaging analyses of the American Revolution fortification at Butts Hill in Portsmouth, Rhode in order to determine whether subterranean wartime structural features such as military barracks can be identified. Results will then be aggregated with previous archaeological and historical information to realize: (1) on-site storyboard exhibit signage that recounts the history of Butts Hill Fort during wartime, as well as (2) a virtual exhibition highlighting archaeological imaging results, historical maps, and satellite/aerial imagery overlaid with historical text in an interactive on-line interface. The proposed dual approach combining traditional on-site public dissemination content with a wide-reaching digital humanities approach will serve to engage local communities and a national virtual audience in celebrating the success of American Independence leading up to the nation’s semiquincentennial.
Grant.ToSupport:
Archaeological fieldwork at the
Revolutionary-era Butts Hill fortification and the creation of on-site exhibit
signage and a virtual exhibition in Portsmouth, Rhode Island.

Grant.ProjectTitle: Writers of Interwar Vienna
Grant.ProjectDesc: This compendium of Austrian literature in translation offers English-language readers their first comprehensive introduction to some of Vienna’s finest but overlooked writers from the early twentieth century, a selection including Vicki Baum, Maria Leitner, Mela Hartwig, Maria Lazar, Veza Canetti, Lili Gru¨n, and Hilde Spiel, among others. Preceding the volume’s essays and excerpts, a lengthy introduction situates readers within the heady context of interwar Vienna’s social experiments—experiments that have not been invalidated by the fact that we know the period ended in a National Socialist takeover. This anthology will provide a much-needed, even urgent corrective to the simplified view of early twentieth century Austrian culture, society and history that has become dominant. It will restore the complex, vibrant fabric of interwoven views and voices that has faded into uniformity.
Grant.ToSupport: Editing and translating a compendium of Austrian literature from the years between World War I and World War II.

Grant.ProjectTitle: "A Garden for Liberty: Celebrating Taunton’s Revolutionary Spirit"
Grant.Program: Cooperative Agreements and Special Projects (Challenge Grants)
Grant.ProjectDesc: In commemoration of America’s 250th anniversary, the Old Colony History Museum proposes the development of a landscaped garden and expanded parking area to honor Robert Treat Paine, a Taunton resident and signer of the Declaration of Independence. This project aims to enhance public engagement with Taunton’s rich Revolutionary history by creating a welcoming space for reflection, education, and community gatherings.
Grant.ToSupport:
Development of a landscaped garden to honor
Declaration of Independence signer Robert Treat Paine in Taunton, Massachusetts.

Grant.ProjectTitle: Sharing Philadelphia’s History for the Semiquincentennial
Grant.Program: Cooperative Agreements and Special Projects (Challenge Grants)
Grant.ProjectDesc: This grant would support a multifaceted project engaging the Atwater Kent Collection (AKC), Philadelphia’s city history collection, in programming celebrating the nation’s 250th anniversary—in collaboration with community partner organizations, large and small, throughout the Philadelphia area, where the Declaration of Independence was signed. The project will boost the accessibility of the AKC and increase the presence of these cultural resources in the community, sharing objects and stories—particularly through a series of traveling/community exhibit displays during this national celebration period—as a way for Philadelphians and visitors to gain a deeper appreciation for the city’s role in our country’s history. Drexel University is the steward of the AKC (the collection of the former Philadelphia History Museum, which closed in 2018): 133,000-plus objects reflecting more than 350 years of Philadelphia—American—history.
Grant.ToSupport:
A series of traveling
exhibitions in the Philadelphia area celebrating the nation's 250th anniversary using historic materials from the Atwater Kent Collection from the former Philadelphia
History Museum, Pennsylvania.

Grant.ProjectTitle: CSRC Visiting Scholars
Grant.Program: Cooperative Agreements and Special Projects (Public Programs)
Grant.ProjectDesc: The Center for the Study of Religion and Conflict (CSRC) at Arizona State University is requesting emergency financial support in the form of an NEH Chairman’s Grant for $30,000 to fund the Center’s Visiting Scholars Program. This funding is specifically requested to provide urgent support for the Center’s artist-in-residence, Dr. Mohammad Yousof Asefi. Dr Asefi’s artwork provides a basis upon which the Center is able to offer humanities-based programming about the intersection of religion, culture, and conflict. His painting has been informed by his having lived in Afghanistan both under Taliban rule and during the US military mission in Afghanistan. The Center has up to now been able to support Dr. Asefi’s residency only through the generosity of private donors. That funding, however, will run out in late 2025. A Chairman’s Grant in the amount requested would enable CSRC to fund the remainder of his two-year residency.
Grant.ToSupport: No to support statement

Grant.ProjectTitle: Painting the Nature of America
Grant.Program: Cooperative Agreements and Special Projects (Challenge Grants)
Grant.ProjectDesc: The Thomas Cole National Historic Site is requesting a Celebrate America! Grant of $25,000 to support the semiquincentennial initiative, “Painting the Nature of America,” in honor of the founding of the county. This American history and art humanities public project will be presented throughout 2026 at the TCNHS, the home of American landscape painting, where the artist Thomas Cole lived and worked in Catskill, New York. "Painting the Nature of America” will include three temporary exhibits with community programs presenting historic and contemporary American art and related programming that celebrates the stunning natural landscape of the United States. The project will explore the enduring influence of Thomas Cole’s American landscape paintings, which gave rise to the newly independent country's identity of America the beautiful. As we mark the nation’s 250th anniversary, Cole’s vision of this place in all its natural beauty continues to inspire and engage generations today.
Grant.ToSupport:
An exhibition at the Thomas Cole Historic House,
Catskill, New York, of the heroic landscapes of Thomas Cole and related
painters that became iconic expressions of the nation’s identity as America the
beautiful.

Grant.ProjectTitle: Founding Statesman: John Jay and the Creation of the United States
Grant.ProjectDesc: I am applying for a Chairman’s Award, with the purpose of completing a significant book manuscript, Founding Statesman: John Jay and the Creation of the United States. Jay was an indispensable figure in the founding of the U.S., serving as President of Congress, Diplomat to Spain, Negotiator of the 1783 Paris Peace Treaty, Secretary of Foreign Affairs, First Chief Justice of the Supreme Court, Special Minister to Great Britain, and Governor of New York. Jay’s story is vitally important for understanding the American Founding, and with the 250th anniversary of independence on the horizon a new biography will make an important contribution at a time when citizens are increasingly interested in the Founding era. The grant will last six months, January-June 2026. The funds would allow for the course release and time necessary to complete the manuscript. The result of the grant would be to have a finalized manuscript ready to submit to a press at the end of the granting period.
Grant.ToSupport: Research and writing towards a biography of John Jay (1745-1829), U.S. diplomat and first Chief Justice of the Supreme Court.

Grant.Institution: Victims of Communism Memorial Foundation, Inc.
Grant.ProjectTitle: Honor the Declaration of Independence’s Global Impact - Celebrate America’s 250th
Grant.ProjectDesc: The Victims of Communism Memorial Foundation (VOC) will honor the legacy of the Declaration of Independence with an essay contest that will teach students about freedom movements that directly cited or paraphrased the Declaration of Independence. This will demonstrate to citizens and students the exceptional nature of the American “experiment” in self-government and ordered liberty. The Foundation will recognize up to 52 outstanding student essays that focus attention on how the Declaration of Independence influenced declarations, speeches, and other political writing in foreign contexts during the 20th century. We are especially interested in short essays that focus on those seeking freedom from communist and Marxist systems.
Grant.ToSupport: An essay contest for high school and college students, recognizing 52 essays on how the Declaration of Independence influenced declarations, speeches, and other political writing in foreign contexts during the twentieth century.

Participant.Institution: Victims of Communism Memorial Foundation, Inc.

Grant.ProjectTitle: American Federalism at 250: the Enduring Legacy of the Federal Idea in a Divided Nation
Grant.ProjectDesc: American federalism is often considered the revolutionary generation’s unique contribution to democratic theory and practice. Today, more than half the world’s population lives in some kind of federal system. Nearly 250 years ago, the idea of dividing sovereignty across different tiers of government was viewed as radical, even impossible. The American Revolution gave rise to a profound rethinking of political power, and it culminated in a new form of government, what Madison called “The Compound Republic.” Highly imperfect, and vigorously debated, it was accepted on the assumption that it would secure a few key advantages: checking centralized power, keeping government close to the people, and accommodating diversity in a pluralistic society. This book project traces the intellectual and constitutional history of these ideals and explains the surprising persistence of the federal idea in the United States, despite recurring—and often overstated—claims of its demise.
Grant.ToSupport: Research and writing towards a book on the history and future of American federalism.

Grant.Institution: Lillian and Albert Small Capital Jewish Museum, Inc.
Grant.ProjectTitle: Securing the Lillian and Albert Small Capital Jewish Museum.
Grant.ProjectDesc: The Museum fulfills its mission by remaining open to the public, and therefore has extensive security measures in place. Following the tragic shooting of two individuals outside the Museum on May 21, 2025, the Museum must now further enhance its security, significantly increasing those costs. On-site security personnel is, by far, the largest expense and to which this grant will be applied. The Museum will contract a temporary senior-level professional for a few weeks before making a more permanent hire. This professional will manage and coordinate the guard force and relationships with MPD and FBI. We will also hire a new contracted security firm and add additional guards to our daily security. By doing so, we anticipate security costs to double. It is with these enhancements that we can ensure our staff, collection, and visitors are and feel safe, so that we can bring Jewish history, art, language, and religion to all who visit  our institution.
Grant.ToSupport: No to support statement

Participant.Institution: Lillian and Albert Small Capital Jewish Museum, Inc.

Grant.ProjectTitle: The History and Tradition of Protecting Parental Rights in the United States
Grant.ProjectDesc: In Pierce v. Society of Sisters (1925), the United States Supreme Court declared that there is an unenumerated but judicially enforceable constitutional right for parents to “direct the upbringing and education” of their children.  The justices asserted that there is a long history of jurists and lawmakers respecting this right in the Anglo-American tradition, but they did not offer much evidence to support this claim.  A few scholars have touched on this history of this right in America, but none have done so in a comprehensive manner.    I propose to write a 45,000-word law review article providing a great deal of evidence to support these justices’ claim. I’ll pay special attention to the founders’ views on this subject because they created America’s constitutional order, the very order under which we still live.
Grant.ToSupport: No to support statement

Grant.ProjectTitle: Profiles in Citizenship: The Women Architects of American Identity
Grant.ProjectDesc: The question of what makes an American citizen is perhaps more important now than ever before. While modern debates center legal citizenship, these debates neglect the social and interpersonal dimensions of citizenship that have long provided the bedrock for American society. To refocus the conversation on citizenship and provide a theoretical grounding for this facet of citizenship in early American history, this project examines the writings of four women, Abigail Adams, Mercy Otis Warren, Judith Sargent Murray, and Phillis Wheatley, as important contributions to the political thought of the American Founding. This project focuses on how, by merit of their social roles as women, the writings of Adams, Warren, Murray, and Wheatley reveal new ways of conceptualizing American citizenship—namely, that complete citizenship requires not only legal grounding, but also community-based belonging, civic virtue, participation in collective memory, and commitment to social duties.
Grant.ToSupport: Research and writing toward a book on concepts of American citizenship through the writings of four women of the Founding Era.

Grant.ProjectTitle: George Washington and the Politics of Honor
Grant.ProjectDesc: I intend to write a scholarly book on George Washington's understanding of the role of honor in politics.  The work is projected to include the following chapters: 1) An introduction, making the case for the study of honor. 2) A chapter on Washington's understanding of honor as an inducement to, and as a guide in conducting oneself in, offices of high political responsibility. 3) A chapter on honor and the office of the presidency. 4) A chapter on national honor and dignity. 5)A chapter on the honor due to God, or on the role of religion in politics. 6) A conclusion on the challenges of honoring Washington today, in view of recent criticisms of him and the Founders more generally for their role in injustices such as slavery.
Grant.ToSupport: Research and writing toward a book on George Washington's understanding of the role of honor in politics.

Grant.ProjectTitle: Newport's Three Revolutions Exhibition
Grant.Program: Cooperative Agreements and Special Projects (Challenge Grants)
Grant.ProjectDesc: In 2026, the Newport Historical Society will design and build a new temporary exhibition, "Newport’s Three Revolutions." This immersive experience guides visitors through three pivotal periods of change in the city between 1775 and 1783: Revolutionary, British, and French rule.  The exhibit will feature 18th-century artifacts from the Newport Historical Society collections, all centered in primary source research. Additionally, it explores the lasting legacies of Newport's revolutionary experience, tracing its impact through the city's 19th, 20th, and 21st-century histories. This project offers a unique opportunity to understand how these formative years continue to shape Newport, providing valuable insights into the broader American narrative. The exhibition will be open free-of-charge to the public from February to December 2026.
Grant.ToSupport:
An exhibition on the history of Newport, Rhode Island,
during successive rule and occupation by American Revolutionary, British, and
French forces from 1775-1781.

Grant.ProjectTitle: The Bible in the Political Culture of the American Founding
Grant.ProjectDesc: The Bible is an important, yet understudied, source of influence on the American founders that must be studied alongside other intellectual influences, such as British constitutionalism, Enlightenment liberalism, and classical and civic republicanism, if one wants to understand the broad range of ideas that informed the founding generation's political thought and practice. This grant will be used to research and write several chapters that will be added to a revised and expanded edition of my book, Reading the Bible with the Founding Fathers (Oxford University Press). The chapters will explore biblical influences on the founders' views of human nature and on the American constitutional tradition and the diverse uses of the Bible in the political rhetoric of the founding era.
Grant.ToSupport: Research and writing towards a book on the place of the Bible in the political thought of the American founders.

Grant.ProjectTitle: Developing Educational and Community Programs at the Speaker’s House
Grant.Program: Cooperative Agreements and Special Projects (Challenge Grants)
Grant.ProjectDesc: Historic Trappe will launch a new slate of public humanities programming at the Speaker’s House, the restored home of Frederick Muhlenberg, first Speaker of the U.S. House of Representatives. Timed to coincide with the 250th anniversary of American independence and the grand opening of the house in April 2026, this project will engage public audiences with the political, religious, and domestic life of the early American republic. Educational programs include archaeology workshops for children and families; immersive foodways demonstrations in the restored kitchen; a lecture series led by nationally recognized scholars; and curriculum-aligned field trips that teach civic history through site-based interpretation.
Grant.ToSupport:
Lecture series, family programs, and school fieldtrips
about the involvement of the Muhlenberg family in the Revolutionary period to
be held at the restored home of Frederick Muhlenberg (1750-1801), first Speaker
of the U.S. House of Representatives, in Trappe, Pennsylvania.

Grant.ProjectTitle: Publius Reconsidered: A New and Comprehensive Reading of "The Federalist"
Grant.ProjectDesc: Secondary authors often fail to  place The Federalist back in its dramatic context: both with regard to debates over ratification and in response to Anti-federalist arguments critical of the Constitution. The Anti-federalists, firing the first shots, prompted Publius’ informed essays, and that back-and-forth provides the framework for my interpretation of The Federalist. The proposed work accomplishes two things: it provides readers with an essay by essay analysis of all 85 Federalist Papers, and it deepens the readers’ sense of the historical context and debates surrounding adoption of the Constitution. Only by placing The Federalist in its dramatic context can we properly understand the underlying issues that resonate in American politics to this day.
Grant.ToSupport: Research and writing of a book on the Federalist Papers, placing them in their historical and political context.

Grant.Institution: Friends of Washington Crossing Park, Inc.
Grant.ProjectTitle: Living History at Washington Crossing Historic Park
Grant.Program: Cooperative Agreements and Special Projects (Challenge Grants)
Grant.ProjectDesc: Friends of Washington Crossing Park will produce dynamic living history programs at Washington Crossing Historic Park throughout 2026, including the 250th anniversary of Washington's crossing of the Delaware, an event that changed the course of the American Revolution.
Grant.ToSupport:
Costs for consultants and materials to expand and
enhance living history programs and reenactments of George Washington’s crossing
the Delaware River in 2025 and 2026, in Washington Crossing, Pennsylvania.

Participant.Institution: Friends of Washington Crossing Park, Inc.

Grant.ProjectTitle: NEH Chairman's Grant - Institute for the Study of Contemporary Antisemitism Conference
Grant.ProjectDesc: With the funding assistance of the National Endowment of the Humanities, Indiana University’s Institute for the Study of Contemporary Antisemitism (ISCA) is prepared to organize an important conference in the coming academic year to raise questions related to major developments in campus antisemitism since October 7, 2023.
Grant.ToSupport: No to support statement

Grant.ProjectTitle: 50 Objects for the 250th
Grant.Program: Cooperative Agreements and Special Projects (Challenge Grants)
Grant.ProjectDesc: In recognition of the 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence and the founding of the United States, the Vermont Historical Society will curate a public exhibit and related publication focused on 50 objects that tell of Vermont’s history and relationship with the republic from its founding. This project will engage Vermonters from across the state in exploring Vermont’s history, as told by objects from our collection. The project will highlight the importance of preserving Vermont’s treasures to telling the story of Vermont as a part of a new nation.
Grant.ToSupport:
An exhibition and related publication on documents and
artifacts related to the American Revolution in Vermont at the Vermont History
Center in Barre, Vermont.

Grant.ProjectTitle: Just War: A Military History
Grant.ProjectDesc: Research and drafting of new one volume history of moral reasoning in warfare entitled Just War: a Military History. Part I provides a new history of major Ancient, Medieval, and early Modern developments in Just War discourses that shaped the American founding. Part II focuses on the American context. One chapter examines the American Revolution in its trans-continental context, followed by chapters examining major shifts in moral argument and their relationship to American military strategies from the Civil War to the War on Terror. A conclusion restates the major claim—that moral reasoning precedes and directly shapes policy and strategy—and emphasizes that moral considerations operate to direct combat actions. The resulting history will establish the practical impact of moral reasoning upon military action.
Grant.ToSupport: Research and writing toward a history of just war theory, from late antiquity to the War on Terror.

Grant.ProjectTitle: The Survey Course in Humanities Majors in American Higher Education
Grant.ProjectDesc: Researching and writing a book about (1) the experience of teaching an old-fashioned, reading-intensive survey course on the history of the novel; (2) an account of the philosophical and social purposes of the novel in particular and the humanities in general; and (3) an account of research into previous decades of syllabi for humanities courses in American academia.
Grant.ToSupport: Research and writing toward a book on changes in how literature has been taught in American college classrooms.

Grant.ProjectTitle: Celebrate America: 250 Years of Freedom
Grant.Program: Cooperative Agreements and Special Projects (Challenge Grants)
Grant.ProjectDesc: The signers of the Declaration of Independence risked their lives, their homes, and their families by daring to revolt against Great Britian. If they had been captured by the British, the basic rights and liberties Americans expect in a court trial would not have been available to them without the protections guaranteed in the Constitution’s Bill of Rights. In this exploration of the 250th anniversary of American freedom teachers help students to realize that they become producers of knowledge and content creators when they explore the humanities. Teachers and students gather and interpret information for new audiences. Furthermore, students, teachers, and audience members realize that the American Revolution was not a forgone conclusion, it was controversial, and America could have easily lost the war.
Grant.ToSupport:
A collaboration between Ball State University, Indiana,
and the Gallia-Vinton Educational Service Center, Ohio, to provide an
educational program and fieldtrip to Philadelphia for Ohio teachers and
students to learn more about the Declaration of Independence and the American
Revolution.

Grant.ProjectTitle: The Golden Age of Architecture in Asheville: 1895-1935
Grant.Program: Cooperative Agreements and Special Projects (Challenge Grants)
Grant.ProjectDesc: The Asheville Art Museum requests $25,000 to support the installation and presentation of the exhibition "The Golden Age of Architecture in Asheville: 1895-1935" (working title), exploring how the built environment of Asheville, North Carolina, was shaped by the artistic vision of architects Douglas D. Ellington and Richard Sharp Smith & Albert Heath Carrier during the first three decades of the 20th century, and how this architectural vision then influenced the field of architecture nationally. This exhibition is in celebration of our nation’s Semiquincentennial (America 250) and will be accompanied by a robust array of public educational programming. This project seeks to deepen public understanding of architectural heritage, preservation, and civic identity through this exhibition and public engagement.
Grant.ToSupport:
An exhibition celebrating Asheville’s Art Deco
architecture at the Asheville Art Museum, North Carolina.

Grant.Institution: Charlotte Mason Educational Center of Pennsylvania
Grant.ProjectTitle: The CMEC TBG Project
Grant.ProjectDesc: The mission of the CMEC is to research and promote Charlotte Mason’s educational philosophy  and methods, provide a program of study and resources for a liberal education, and create a community that grows as person, parent, and teacher.
